one_liner: Pure-Python DNS toolkit; gevent's wrapper for it beat gevent's c-ares resolver on the maintainer's macOS, but lost on Linux.
what_it_does: dnspython is a DNS toolkit for Python. Its high-level resolver (dns.resolver.resolve, with dns.asyncresolver for asyncio and Trio) returns answer RRsets, and low-level classes handle messages, names, rdata, zones, zone transfers, dynamic updates, TSIG, EDNS0 and DNSSEC. It is not a drop-in for the c-ares C API. The speed comparison is through gevent: the gevent.resolver.dnspython backend implements the socket functions (gethostbyname, getaddrinfo, gethostbyaddr, getnameinfo) on top of dnspython, as an alternative to the gevent.resolver.ares backend.
how_it_is_fast: There is no new algorithm; the measured win comes from how gevent uses dnspython. gevent attaches a TTL-respecting, thread-safe dns.resolver.LRUCache to one module-global dnspython resolver (dnspython caches nothing by default), so repeat lookups are answered in-process with no network round trip; the maintainer reported that turning the cache on cut the parallel run from 0.18-0.29 s to 0.05-0.07 s. Under gevent monkey-patching, dnspython's pure-Python sockets become cooperative, so 100 greenlet lookups overlap: on the maintainer's machine the parallel run took 16-22% of the sequential time, against 65-82% for c-ares. The benchmark harness also creates a new gevent c-ares Resolver, and so a new c-ares channel, inside every timed call, while each new dnspython Resolver reuses the shared, already-warm resolver.
when_to_use: gevent programs that make many concurrent lookups, where the default threaded resolver is not acceptable and you have measured gevent's c-ares resolver as slow on your own platform (the published win is from macOS only).
Workloads that look up the same names many times, where an in-process cache that obeys DNS TTLs, can be sized (set_max_size) and can be flushed is useful.
Anything beyond A/AAAA lookups: arbitrary record types, zone transfers, dynamic updates, TSIG, EDNS0, DNSSEC, and DNS over HTTPS, TLS or QUIC through optional extras.
asyncio or Trio code that needs a native async resolver (dns.asyncresolver) instead of running getaddrinfo in a thread pool.

PyPy or other deployments where you want no C extension: dnspython has no required dependencies, and gevent's docs call its own c-ares resolver 'extremely experimental on PyPy' with possible interpreter crashes.
when_not_to_use: gevent services on Linux. The only independent rerun of gevent's script (Linux Mint 19.1, CPython 2.7.15rc1, gevent 1.3.7, local dnsmasq) had c-ares at 36.7 us vs dnspython at 100 us per sequential lookup and 32.8 vs 103 us in parallel, so c-ares was about 2.7-3.1x faster (derived from page data).

Uncached lookups against a remote resolver. In the PR's first test (100 lookups against 8.8.8.8), c-ares took 50-53 s and dnspython 156-162 s, so c-ares was about 3x faster; the same user's earlier Linux run with the older script had dnspython at 5.46 s vs c-ares at 0.31 s (best of 5).
When you need system resolution semantics. dnspython does not read /etc/hosts, and its README says socket.getaddrinfo() or socket.gethostbyname() is better for simple forward lookups.

CPU-bound, very high-rate resolution: every response is parsed in Python. Issue #259 showed large A/AAAA answers burning CPU in the old O(n^2) set code; the new set code fixed it, but parsing is still interpreted.

When you need a current number: all measurements are from 2018-2019 (dnspython 1.15-era on Python 2.7/3.6/3.7) and were never re-run. Since c-ares 1.31.0 the c-ares query cache is on by default (gevent now bundles c-ares 1.34.5), which removes the cache asymmetry the old runs depended on.

integration.dependencies: none for the default install (standard library only). Optional extras: dnssec (cryptography), doh (httpcore2, httpx2, h2), doq (aioquic), idna, trio, wmi (Windows only). The benchmarked setup also needs gevent.
integration.min_toolchain: Python 3.10+ (dnspython 2.8.0 and 2.9.0 dev); Python 2 support ended with 1.16.0
integration.platforms: any platform with CPython 3.10+ (package classifiers list POSIX and Windows); gevent's changelog says the dnspython backend works on PyPy
integration.thread_safety: Resolver.resolve() is safe to call from many threads, but changing resolver configuration is not. Cache and LRUCache are thread-safe. Name and Rdata are immutable; Message, Rdataset, RRset and Zone are not locked (VersionedZone is thread-safe).
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — inside gevent it replaces gevent's c-ares resolver behind the same socket-module functions through gevent's resolver setting; as a standalone library its API is unrelated to c-ares, though dns.resolver.override_system_resolver() can patch Python's socket module to use it

gotchas: dnspython's resolver does not cache unless you assign a cache (resolver.cache = dns.resolver.LRUCache()). The gevent benchmark had gevent's LRUCache on, so direct dnspython users without a cache will not see those numbers.

gevent's wrapper adds its own hosts-file layer (reloaded every 300 s) and, by default, extra CNAME queries for aliases. gevent's benchmark turns the alias lookups off for dnspython because c-ares does not do them.
gevent still documents the dnspython resolver as '*experimental*' and says it 'may be removed or modified in the future'; errors and IPv6 scope-ID handling differ from the standard library.
Use 2.6.1 or later: CVE-2023-29483 (GHSA-3rq5-2g8h-59hc, the 'TuDoor' DoS through spoofed responses in the stub resolver) affects versions before 2.6.1.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The catalogued siblings are DNS servers (Unbound, Hickory DNS, Nail, Bundy-DNS, measured against BIND) and QUIC stacks, and none is a client-side Python resolver library. Pick dnspython when resolution or DNS message and zone handling must happen inside a Python process, and pair it with a local caching server such as Unbound; for native code or Linux gevent services, the c-ares baseline is the better-measured choice.
verified_claims_summary: On one unspecified macOS machine with a local dnsmasq that caches everything, gevent's maintainer measured gevent's dnspython resolver ahead of gevent's c-ares resolver: about 2-4.4x on 300 sequential gethostbyname calls and 8.6-13x on 100 parallel greenlet lookups (Feb 2018, dnspython cache off, PyPy 2 5.10 and CPython 2.7/3.6/3.7b1), and 147 us vs 6.56 ms per lookup (about 45x) with gevent's bench_dns_resolver.py on CPython 3.7.0 (Oct 2018, LRUCache on). The result is contested: the same script on Linux Mint 19.1 (CPython 2.7.15rc1) gave c-ares 36.7 us vs dnspython 100 us (c-ares about 2.7x faster); dnspython's per-lookup time was similar on both machines (147 vs 100 us), and c-ares differed about 180x (6.56 ms vs 36.7 us), so the flip comes from c-ares on the macOS setup (all ratios derived from page data; no CPU models given).
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-26; latest PyPI release 2.8.0 on 2025-09-07, 2.9.0 in development) and ISC-licensed pure Python with no required dependencies, so it is easy to adopt; gevent still labels its dnspython backend experimental.
